thread.title: Mello: No FEMA money for blizzard
thread.title_full: Mello: No FEMA money for blizzard

author: ohtadmin
title: Mello: No FEMA money for blizzard
text:
Town Administrator Ed Mello briefed the town council about the federal government’s denial of a requested disaster declaration to help offset costs associated with the February blizzard.
On July 2, President Donald Trump denied the request from Gov. Dan McKee, which means the Federal Emergency Management Agency will not reimburse cities and towns for certain expenses related to the storm.
Mello had been prepared to submit a request of $361,000 to FEMA, including $23,640 in overtime pay and $265,000 to replace two generators destroyed during the storm.
“These two items remain outstanding with our insurance carrier,” he reported.
McKee, who accused Trump of playing partisan politics during an event when lives were at risk, has appealed the decision.
“The Trump administration’s denial of Rhode Island’s disaster declaration appears to be yet another case of the White House putting politics ahead of people,” he said. The congressional delegation of Rhode Island also condemned Trump by saying his denial was “a petty move that hurts people.”
U.S. Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse, to ensure this doesn’t happen in the future, have introduced the Disaster Relief Fairness Act. Major disasters under current law are declared pursuant to Section 401 of the Stafford Act. One key factor is a comparison of the cost of the disaster’s impact to the state’s ability to handle the event, a metric typically calculated by multiplying the per capita indicator by the state’s population. While the declaration process included in Section 401 leaves significant discretion to the president, said Reed’s office, no other president has ever before made politics the deciding factor.
Trump, according to the Association Press, “has approved more than three-fourths of the requests from states that voted for him in the 2024 election but less than half the requests from states that did not.”
The Reed-Whitehouse bill would prevent a president from maliciously denying disaster assistance to states and communities when they have met the criteria to qualify.
“Time and again, President Trump has shown that he can’t see past his own personal grievances and partisan biases when it comes to providing disaster aid,” said Reed, a Jamestown resident. “The Disaster Relief Fairness Act would ensure that the disaster declaration process is both impartial and consistent. Our bill would prevent Trump from using disaster assistance for political leverage or retribution by ensuring that every request for disaster assistance made during his presidency will be approved as long as it meets FEMA’s established requirements and thresholds. This will guarantee that states and tribes will get the relief they need to fully recover from disasters.”
On Feb. 22-23, Rhode Island was hit by a blizzard that shut down the state for days. More than 3 feet of snow fell on the state in a 24-hour period, which is the highest one-day snowfall on record for Rhode Island. The storm hit Rhode Island with the intensity of a Category 2 hurricane, with winds up to 74 miles per hour.
The historic blizzard caused more than $19.3 million in damage across Rhode Island, which Reed said amounted to more than nine times the threshold required for a disaster declaration under Federal Emergency Management Agency guidelines.
